solicitation

/suh-lis-ih-TAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Solicitation means the act of asking for or trying to obtain something, such as support, donations, or business.

Every autumn the booster club's solicitation of local businesses fills the team's equipment budget for the season.

Example

The children's hospital's spring solicitation — a mailed letter asking longtime supporters for donations toward a new playroom — raised more money than any campaign in its history.

The letter exists for one purpose: to ask. An organized act of asking supporters for money or help is precisely what a solicitation is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

appeal: An appeal is a direct, open request for help or support — an appeal for volunteers, a flood-relief appeal — and it can be warm and personal. Solicitation is the businesslike, formal word for organized asking, common in law and fundraising. An appeal can come from a friend; a solicitation arrives on letterhead.

entreaty: An entreaty is a heartfelt, urgent plea — something matters greatly and the asker shows it. Solicitation is drier and procedural: the organized act of asking for donations, business, or support. An entreaty begs from the heart; a solicitation asks by form letter.

petition: A petition is a formal request made to an authority, often written and signed by many people. A solicitation runs the other way: an organization asking individuals for money, business, or help. You petition the powerful; solicitations land in your own mailbox.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

offer: something given or proposed without being asked for

rebuff: a blunt rejection of an approach or request

Where it sits · how intense the asking becomes

hint → solicitation → supplication

hint vs. solicitation: A hint only gestures at what you want; a solicitation asks for it openly and on purpose.

supplication vs. solicitation: A supplication is far more intense than a solicitation — it is desperate, humble begging.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — solicit-: to stir up, ask earnestly (Latin sollicitare, from sollus 'whole' + citare 'to rouse, set in motion')

Suffix — -ation: act or process of

Put it together: Sollicitare meant 'to stir the whole thing up' — to rouse someone into responding. Add -ation and you get the act of stirring someone to respond: an earnest, deliberate ask.

Use the root in a new word: recite: Each morning the actor would recite his lines in the empty theater — literally 'setting them in motion again' out loud.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Formal / business & legal

Solicitation lives in formal territory: 'No Solicitation' signs on office doors, fundraising letters, legal filings about the solicitation of investors. Don't confuse it with the look-alike solicitude, which means anxious concern for someone's well-being — asking versus caring.
